name: Penne
look: Short smooth tube with both ends cut on the diagonal, like a quill nib.
fact: Named after the quill pen. In 1865 Giovanni Battista Capurro, near Genoa, patented a machine that cut the diagonal ends without crushing the tube.

name: Penne rigate
look: Short tube cut on the diagonal, with fine ridges running along the outside.
fact: Rigate simply means ridged: the grooves give tomato sauce more grip, which is why this version far outsells smooth penne.

name: Pennette
look: A slimmer, shorter penne, usually ridged.
fact: The smaller penne you see in quick weeknight sauces and bakes; its thin walls cook a couple of minutes faster than full-size penne.

name: Mezze penne
look: Penne of normal width but roughly half the length, smooth or ridged.
fact: Cutting penne short makes pieces about the size of a chickpea or a diced vegetable, so they mix evenly into chunky sauces and thick soups.

name: Pennoni
look: Oversized penne: a wide, long diagonal-cut tube, smooth or ridged.
fact: The augmentative of penne. The wide bore lets chunky ragù get inside, and the tubes are sturdy enough to bake.

name: Penne a candela
look: Long, slender smooth tube with quill-cut ends, longer than ordinary penne.
fact: A quill-cut relative of Naples' long smooth "candle" tubes; the length and smooth wall suit slow-cooked Neapolitan sauces.

name: Trenne
look: Penne-like diagonal-cut tube with a triangular rather than round cross-section.
fact: Three flat faces and sharp corners give trenne a firmer bite than round penne; the smaller size is sold as trennette.

name: Garganelli
look: Small egg-pasta square rolled corner to corner into a ridged quill with a visible overlapping seam.
fact: Made by rolling squares of egg dough around a stick over a ridged comb (pettine). Legend says a Romagna cook invented them when the tortellini filling went missing.

name: Macarrones
look: Short ridged tube with diagonal ends, essentially Spanish penne.
fact: In Spain "macarrones" means short quill-cut tubes, and macarrones con chorizo y tomate is a staple of home cooking.

name: Maccheroni
look: Plain short straight tube of medium width, usually smooth.
fact: For centuries, especially in the south, "maccheroni" meant dried pasta in general; only later did it settle on short tubes. The word's origin is still disputed.

name: Maccheroncini
look: Slim short straight tube, narrower than maccheroni.
fact: In most of Italy the word means slim short tubes, but in Campofilone in the Marche "maccheroncini" are hair-fine egg strands, a completely different pasta.

name: Ziti
look: Smooth straight-cut tube of medium width, sold short or snapped from long lengths.
fact: The classic wedding pasta of Naples. Traditionally made as long tubes and snapped by hand before cooking; pre-cut "ziti tagliati" came later.

name: Cannolicchi
look: Short straight tube, smooth or ridged, a size up from soup tubetti.
fact: The name comes from canna, a reed or pipe, and is also the Italian word for razor clams, which have the same narrow tubular look.

name: Ditali
look: Short stubby tube shaped like an open-ended thimble, smooth or ridged.
fact: The middle size of the thimble family, between tiny ditalini and big ditaloni; made for legume soups thick enough to eat with a fork.

name: Ditaloni
look: Wide, short thimble-like tube, the largest of the ditali family.
fact: A larger ditalini whose name means "big thimbles". A favourite for pasta e fagioli because beans lodge inside the wide tube.

name: Canneroni
look: Short, wide straight tube, the larger sibling of cannolicchi.
fact: A southern soup tube scaled up: wide enough to catch chickpeas and beans, and sturdy enough for thick vegetable sauces.

name: Kofto makaronaki
look: Small short smooth tube, straight or very slightly curved.
fact: The everyday short tube of Greek kitchens, simmered directly in the sauce for one-pot dishes such as octopus with pasta.

name: Rigatoni
look: Wide straight-cut tube with deep lengthwise ridges.
fact: From rigato, "ridged": the grooves and wide bore were made for meaty sauces to lodge in. It is the tube of Roman cooking, from carbonara to pajata.

name: Mezzi rigatoni
look: Rigatoni of full width but about half the length.
fact: The shorter barrel is easier to spear and fills completely with sauce, which makes it popular for chunky vegetable and sausage sauces.

name: Tortiglioni
look: Rigatoni-sized tube whose ridges spiral around the barrel.
fact: Unlike rigatoni, the grooves twist around the tube, so sauce winds through them instead of sitting in straight channels. The name comes from Latin torquere, to twist.

name: Elicoidali
look: Medium straight-cut tube, slimmer than rigatoni, with ridges that curve gently around it.
fact: The name describes the helical ridges. It sits between rigatoni and tortiglioni: narrower than both, with a shallower spiral.

name: Mezze maniche
look: Stubby ridged tube about as wide as rigatoni but only half as long.
fact: Means "half sleeves", like a short-sleeved shirt. In Rome it is a favourite for carbonara, gricia and amatriciana, since the short barrel scoops up bits of guanciale.

name: Sedani
look: Slim, slightly curved ridged tube with straight-cut ends.
fact: Named for the look of a ribbed celery stalk. The smooth version is reportedly older and went by the name denti d'elefante, "elephant's teeth".

name: Sedanini
look: Small, narrow, slightly curved ridged tube.
fact: The diminutive of sedani; its thin walls and narrow bore suit lighter tomato and vegetable sauces rather than heavy ragù.

name: Millerighe
look: Wide straight tube covered in many fine, closely spaced ridges.
fact: The dense fine ridging multiplies the surface area, so the tube holds more sauce on its outside than a rigatone of the same size.

name: Elbow macaroni
look: Small narrow smooth tube bent into a short curve.
fact: The word is far older than the shape: "macaroni" once meant pasta in general. The little elbow became the North American standard for mac and cheese.

name: Gomiti
look: Short tube bent in a tight curve, smooth or ridged, wider than American elbows.
fact: The bend is made in the die: dough is forced out faster on one side of the opening than the other, so the tube curls as it emerges.

name: Chifferi
look: Short, wide tube curved into a half-moon, smooth or ridged.
fact: Named after the Austrian Kipferl, the crescent-shaped pastry it resembles.

name: Gramigna
look: Short, thin hollow strands curled into little hooks and commas.
fact: Named after a wiry weed. In Bologna it is so tied to sausage that gramigna alla salsiccia reads on menus as a single dish.

name: Hörnli
look: Small curved elbow tube, smooth or lightly ridged.
fact: A Swiss comfort staple: Ghackets mit Hörnli pairs it with minced-meat sauce and apple purée, and it is one of the pastas used for Älplermagronen.

name: Paccheri
look: Very large, wide smooth tube that collapses flat when cooked.
fact: Big enough to stuff one by one. The name likely comes from a Neapolitan word for a slap, perhaps for the sound they make when served.

name: Mezzi paccheri
look: Paccheri cut to about half length: a short, very wide smooth tube.
fact: Half-length paccheri hold their shape better in the pan and are easier to eat, so many cooks prefer them for seafood sauces.

name: Bombardoni
look: Oversized ridged tube, wider and longer than rigatoni.
fact: A giant ridged tube made to be filled by hand or tossed with a very chunky ragù.

name: Occhi di lupo
look: Large, thick-walled short tube with a wide round opening.
fact: Named for the wide round bore that stares up from the plate; the thick walls keep it firm in dense sauces and baked dishes.

name: Tufoli
look: Large, wide smooth tube, shorter than cannelloni.
fact: A big southern tube, wide enough to stuff and bake, yet short enough to be boiled and served with a chunky ragù.

name: Calamarata
look: Thick, wide, short smooth rings about the size of sliced squid.
fact: Shaped to mimic rings of calamari and traditionally cooked with real squid, so pasta and seafood are hard to tell apart on the plate.

name: Fusilli
look: Short three-bladed corkscrew.
fact: Named after the fuso, the spindle that dough was once wound around by hand. Machine-made short fusilli only appeared in the 20th century.

name: Fusilloni
look: Oversized fusilli with deep, wide spiral blades.
fact: Simply fusilli scaled up; the deeper blades trap chunks of vegetable or meat that would slide off the standard size.

name: Eliche
look: Short corkscrew with broad, flat blades and an open spiral.
fact: Named after ship and aircraft propellers. Brands often use eliche and fusilli interchangeably; where both are sold, eliche have the wider blades.

name: Rotini
look: Short corkscrew with a tight, compact spiral.
fact: A North American name: the word is not used in Italy, where the same tight corkscrew would be sold as fusilli or eliche.

name: Spirali
look: Short spiral, usually wound more tightly than fusilli.
fact: A loose trade name: many brands use it for corkscrews tighter than classic fusilli, and some for coiled hollow tubes.

name: Fusilli al ferretto
meaning: fusilli made on the little iron
look: Long, loose hand-made spiral, formed by winding a rope of dough around a thin rod.
fact: The ancestor of factory fusilli: a strip of semolina dough is spun around a thin iron rod, then slid off as a springy coil.

name: Riccioli
look: Short twisted strip curled into a loose ringlet.
fact: The name just means "curls", and makers apply it to several short twisted shapes with open spirals.

name: Fusilli bucati
look: Thin hollow tube wound into a short spring.
fact: Bucati means pierced: the coil is a narrow tube, so it catches sauce both in the spiral and through its hollow centre.

name: Fusilli lunghi bucati
look: Spaghetti-length hollow strand curled like a telephone cord.
fact: The factory descendant of hand-wound Neapolitan fusilli: a long hollow strand set in springy coils, often broken into pieces before cooking.

name: Cavatappi
look: Ridged hollow tube bent into a short open helix.
fact: Means "corkscrews": a hollow spiral combining tube and twist. Barilla launched it in the 1960s as cellentani; other makers use the generic name cavatappi.

name: Gemelli
look: Short piece that looks like two strands twisted around each other.
fact: They look like two strands twisted together, but each piece is usually a single S-shaped strand twisted on itself.

name: Casarecce
look: Short strip rolled lengthwise into a loose S-shaped scroll.
fact: The name means "homemade": the shape copies the look of dough rolled by hand around a thin rod, though today it is mostly factory extruded.

name: Strozzapreti
look: Hand-rolled strip of dough twisted into an irregular elongated curl.
fact: Means "priest stranglers". Legend says Romagna housewives made it for the clergy as rent in kind, hoping the greedy priests would choke on it.

name: Trofie
look: Small thin twist of dough with tapered ends, about 3 cm long.
fact: From the Golfo Paradiso coast near Genoa. Each piece is rubbed across the board with the palm into a tight twist; it is the classic partner of pesto genovese.
pairings: pesto with potatoes and green beans

name: Busiate
look: Long, open telephone-cord coil of semolina dough.
fact: From Trapani in western Sicily: each spiral is rolled around a thin rod or reed called a busa, the tool that gave the pasta its name.

name: Fileja
look: Elongated hand-rolled curl, like a loosely closed tube about 10 cm long.
fact: A Calabrian pasta rolled around a thin rod called a dinaculu, which leaves a hollow channel without any extrusion at all.

name: Maccheroni al ferretto
meaning: macaroni made on the little iron
look: Hand-rolled hollow stick of semolina dough, 5 to 15 cm long, with a visible seam.
fact: Across the southern mainland, dough is rolled around a thin square iron rod and slid off as a hollow tube; every area has its own name for it.

name: Minchiareddhi
look: Short hand-rolled hollow stick, a few centimetres long, with a seam.
fact: The ferretto pasta of Salento. It is often cooked together with orecchiette as "maritati", the married pair served at weddings.

name: Maccarrones de busa
look: Hand-rolled hollow strand like a short, thick, rustic bucatino.
fact: Sardinia's version of rod-rolled pasta: semolina dough is wrapped around a knitting needle (busa) to make a long hollow tube.

name: Pasta al ceppo
look: Strip of dough rolled around a stick into a tube that looks like a cinnamon quill.
fact: From the hills of Teramo province: the ceppo was the knitting-needle-like stick each piece was wrapped around. Dried versions are now extruded.

name: Maccheroni alla bobbiese
look: Hand-rolled hollow stick of fresh dough with a seam along its length.
fact: A speciality of Bobbio in the Piacenza hills, where the dough is rolled around a knitting needle; the classic dressing is slow-braised beef stracotto.
